title: Real-world data and real-world evidence in regulatory decision making

items.abstract: <jats:p>Cognitive functioning is critical as in our daily life a host of real-world complex decisions in high-stakes markets have to be made. The decision-making process can be vulnerable to environmental stressors. Summarizing the growing economic and epidemiologic evidence linking air pollution, cognition performance and real-world decision making, we first illustrate key physiological and psychological pathways between air pollution and cognition. We then document the main patterns of air pollution affecting cognitive test performance by type of cognitive tests, gender, window of exposure, age profile, and educational attainment. We further extend to a review of real-world decision making that has been found to be affected by air pollution and the resulting cognitive impairments. Finally, rich implications on environmental health policies are drawn based on existing evaluations of social costs of air pollution.</jats:p>
title: Smog, Cognition and Real-World Decision Making
Simply Rational
subtitle: Decision Making in the Real World

items.abstract: <jats:p>This article delivers a unified approach to building intelligent agents to make real-world decisions by integrating learned world models. We focus on recent research that builds on world-model frameworks, showing that they encapsulate advanced, predictive and rich representations of an agent's environment (Nottingham et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025), and we synthesise recent literature on model-based reinforcement learning, generative modelling, and decision-theoretic planning (Hu &amp; Shu, 2023). Our examination provides evidence that world models are a game changer in terms of an agent's reasoning, flexibility to switch between different tasks and safety in execution, whether an agent is cognitive, embodied, or both, and that they can predict and respond to required changes in behaviour (Ding et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). These models have developed a unified learning paradigm where the perception, prediction, and action components are interlinked, enabling internal simulation, long-horizon planning, and counterfactual reasoning. The results demonstrate that such frameworks enhance sample efficiency and generalisation across different tasks. Moreover, they offer a principled approach to verifiable autonomy, enabling interpretability and bounded control of behaviour using learned predictive dynamics. We argue that learned world models marked a pivotal advancement toward establishing reliable autonomous action in stark, complex environments. They help to bridge the gap between data-driven perception and decision-theoretic control, which is required for engineering next-generation adaptive, safety-critical intelligent systems.</jats:p>
title: Toward Intelligent Agents with Learned World Models for Real-World Decision-Making

items.abstract: Prior research on confidence in perceptual decision making has almost exclusively used simple, static stimuli. While this work has led to many insights, it remains unclear how complex, real-world factors affect confidence judgments. To address this question, we developed a new task where participants watched short video clips and answered questions about their content by typing their answers and providing confidence on a 0-100 scale. We manipulated five variables related to the video clips – affective states induced by the clips (valence and arousal), prior information about the clips (contextual information coming from prior clips from the same movie and whether those clips were in correct or reverse chronological order), and heuristic cues about task difficulty (scene complexity, quantified as the number of people shown). We found that arousal had a U-shaped effect on accuracy but an inverted-U-shaped effect on confidence. In addition, scene complexity, events chronology, and the number of prior clips from the same movie affected confidence, but not accuracy. A second experiment, in which participants chose among a fixed set of options, replicated all these effects except for the effect of events chronology on confidence. These findings demonstrate that a range of factors— including affect, priors, and heuristic information— contribute selectively to confidence under natural viewing conditions. More broadly, these results highlight major differences in how decisions and confidence incorporate information and begin to reveal the possible sources of metacognitive inefficiency.
title: Confidence in real-world decision making
